summary: An April 1st humorous memo about handing out IP numbers on temporary field networks and small events. It is a joke and not a real protocol, though it pokes fun at the practical problems of running such networks.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke describes assigning IP numbers with wooden clothes-pegs. A person reads the peg and enters the network settings by hand.

subtitle: An April 1st joke protocol that hands out IP numbers using clothes-pegs.

tldr.problem: The RFC addresses the challenge of assigning IP numbers at temporary events with many different kinds of computers.
tldr.mechanism: Its peg-dhcp proposal uses labeled wooden pegs as tokens; people read the values and enter configuration by hand.
tldr.outcome: This April 1st RFC describes the peg-based method in a humorous way, including its risks of loss and human error.

today: RFC 2322 is an Informational April 1st joke document about managing IP numbers with physical pegs.

sections.title: The Peg-DHCP Idea
sections.content:
The RFC describes peg-dhcp for field networks and small events that may lack a clear organizing body. Its history section says the approach was first used at the HIP event, where participants brought computers that needed network access.

Instead of relying on a software server for varied IP stacks, organizers used wooden clothes-pegs. Each peg represented an IP number, and clipping it to a network cable made its assignment visible.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo describes a temporary network where people need IP numbers. It uses labeled pegs instead of relying only on computer software.

sections.title: Pegs, Shared Settings, and Issuing Numbers
sections.content:
A peg carries an IP number or, optionally, a network range. A separate paper can list settings shared across a site, such as the network, netmask, gateway, and proxy. Pegs can use different colors for different subnets.

Clients visit the server, receive a peg, and manually transfer its information and the paper's information into their IP stack. When finished, a client may return the peg for possible reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: The peg identifies the assigned number, and a shared note gives other settings. A person types those values into the computer and can return the peg later.

sections.title: Limitations and Security
sections.content:
The RFC notes that pegs can be lost and that their information is plain text readable by anyone. It says private information should not be exchanged through this protocol.

Manual entry can introduce errors. The memo describes one case where a person used the default router's address as their own IP number, disrupting the network for a time.
sections.plainLanguage: A peg can be lost, and anyone can read its information. Typing the wrong number can also disrupt the network.

references.text: Waitzman, D., "Transmission of IP Datagrams on Avian Carriers", RFC 1149, April 1990.
